learning: Iteration 3 (448.7) is the reference. Its s-bend is at 1.0 line losses with max_error at the floor, and iteration 4 showed the 16 mm footprint does not help. If the s-bend improves with stable oscillation, the inertia lever is useful. If oscillation rises above about 0.35, the next step should be a controller change (lower kd or kp), not further inertia reduction.
notes: Iteration 5 package: the Builder's inertia change (body_length 0.12, mass 0.6) on the iteration 3 design. The controller is unchanged from iteration 3, so the only variable is yaw inertia.
rationale: The Builder's proposal changes only inertia: body_length 0.16 to 0.12 and mass 0.8 to 0.6, with sensor_size back at 0.012, sensors at y 0.07, wheel_track 0.09 and wheel_radius 0.03. Iteration 3 is the best raced design (448.7) and has the same sensors, track and footprint, so it is the right reference. Its controller (kp 2.8, ki 0.05, kd 0.5, base_speed 1.5, last_direction) worked on the oval (20 of 20, max_error 0.025) and left the s-bend at 1.0 line losses with max_error at the 0.06 floor. Iteration 4 showed that the 16 mm footprint lowers the score, so it is not used. I accept the geometry as proposed. Yaw inertia falls from about 0.0027 to about 0.0014 kg m^2, so the same wheel difference should turn the robot faster. That could also raise oscillation, which was 0.32 on the s-bend in iteration 3. For that reason I keep the iteration 3 controller unchanged. Changing only the inertia means any change in the outcome can be attributed to it. The 0.6 kg mass also lowers the load, so base_speed 1.5 should still finish the oval in under 3 s. Expected, not measured: s-bend line losses below 1.0 and progress above 0.68, with steering_oscillation under about 0.35. Risk: a lighter, shorter body may oscillate more on the oval and slip more under acceleration, so steering_oscillation and oval finish rate must be checked.
